name: Kakeya Toranpu
description: Kakeya Toranpu (also known as Etori) is a unique and rare trick-taking game native to Kakeya Town, Shimane Prefecture, Japan. It utilizes a standard 52-card deck but introduces a 'Master Card' called the 'Rensho' (usually the Ace of Spades). The game features fixed partnerships and a scoring system based on Go stones, representing a rare survival of localized Japanese card game culture from the Edo period influence.

overview.description: Kakeya Toranpu (also known as Etori) is a unique and rare trick-taking game native to Kakeya Town, Shimane Prefecture, Japan. It utilizes a standard 52-card deck but introduces a 'Master Card' called the 'Rensho' (usually the Ace of Spades). The game features fixed partnerships and a scoring system based on Go stones, representing a rare survival of localized Japanese card game culture from the Edo period influence.

history.origins: Believed to have been introduced to Kakeya Town in the mid-18th century by a localized doctor who returned from Nagasaki (the only port open to Westerners during the Sakoku era). It resembles early Portuguese 'Hombre' or 'Renette' variants.
timeline: 1750s: Game rules brought to Kakeya Town.
1800s-1900s: Becomes a localized community staple, played during regional festivals.
2004: Recognized as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Unnan City.
Present: Actively preserved by the Kakeya Toranpu Preservation Society.
history.cultural: An extraordinary example of how Western card games were adapted into Japanese village life before the Meiji Restoration.
history.evolution: The game's use of 'Go stones' for scoring and its specific partnership draw (using sticks) are cultural adaptations unique to the town.

setup.players: 4 or 6 players. In 6-player games, two players sit out each round as dealers.
setup.deck: Standard 52-card deck. Aces are high, 2s are low.
setup.dealing: Two players (the Kubariban) deal the entire deck. Each active player gets 13 cards.
setup.equipment: Standard cards, Go stones for scoring, lottery sticks for partnership selection

rules.objective: Win 'Face Cards' (J-Q-K-A) in tricks. The team that captures 9 or more of the 16 face cards wins a Go stone from their opponents.
rules.gameplay:
1. Players draw lottery sticks to determine partnerships.
2. Trump (Kiri) is determined by a cut or rotation.
3. Must follow suit if possible; if not, any card can be played.
4. **Scoring**: Only Face cards (16 total) matter. Winning 9-11 = 1 stone, 12-15 = 2 stones, 16 (All) = 4 stones.
keyRules: The Rensho (usually Ace of Spades) is the highest card and wins any trick it is played to
Players draw lottery sticks to determine partnerships
Trump is determined by cut or rotation
Only Jacks, Queens, Kings, and Aces (16 total) count for scoring
Game ends when a team loses all 5 starting Go stones

strategy.basic: Prioritize capturing Jacks and Queens early, as they are easier to 'snatch' than Kings and Aces. Keep your Rensho until you can capture a trick containing multiple face cards.
strategy.intermediate: Rensho Timing: If your partner leads a plain suit and an opponent plays a King, that is the perfect time to play the Rensho to secure a high-value trick.
strategy.advanced: Bleeding the Deck: Like Bridge, lead trumps early to exhaust the opponents, then use your remaining long suits to walk home with the scoring face cards.
tips: The Rensho (Ace of Spades) is not a trump card; it belongs to the spade suit but outranks trumps if played to a trick.
Watch the dealers in a 6-player game; they aren't playing, but their absence from the trick-taking changes the distribution of cards.

synthesis.shortDescription: A rare Japanese trick-taking game from Shimane Prefecture featuring the powerful Rensho card and Go stone scoring. A living piece of cultural heritage.
